strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: jointly generating synchronized audio and video while controlling visual identity, voice timbre, and spatial structure. Integrating these capabilities within one model has practical value beyond video-only control.

The architecture is coherent: modality-specific branches inject control features into a frozen joint diffusion backbone through zero-initialized projections. Retaining the backbone’s cross-modal attention while specializing the control branches is a reasonable design.

Depth-control results are promising. Table 2 reports depth MAE ×100 of 4.52 versus VACE’s 5.35, with improved subject DINO similarity and dynamic degree. The qualitative examples also illustrate useful identity preservation and structural conditioning.

The evaluation includes visual quality, synchronization, structural fidelity, speech metrics, and a human study. Reporting training resources and explicitly using non-overlapping reference-audio and target segments are helpful implementation details.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the proposed method’s contribution from the strong LTX-2 19B backbone. There is no quantitative comparison against the backbone or a straightforward control-adapter implementation on the same backbone, and no architectural ablation of MMCU, dual-stream injection, or removal of cross-modal attention within the branches. Comparisons with different-generation talking-head and video-control systems establish useful capabilities but cannot establish that the proposed architecture causes the gains.

Evidence for the central claim of composable, independent multimodal control is insufficient. Figure 7 only qualitatively toggles guidance scales between zero and one; it does not measure continuous strength adjustment or interference between voice and visual identity. Appendix B evaluates image-plus-audio conditioning, but there is no quantitative test combining timbre, identity, and structural control simultaneously. Pose adherence is also evaluated only qualitatively.

Voice-timbre preservation lacks a meaningful comparative evaluation. Table S2 reports SIM-o of 0.2574, UTMOS of 3.49, and two WER aggregates on 150 samples, without an uncontrolled backbone, voice-conditioning baseline, or reference-audio calibration. These standalone measurements do not establish how much the audio branch improves speaker fidelity or whether it preserves naturalness and synchronization while doing so.

As an Algorithms/General submission, the methodological originality is limited relative to the claims. Masked latent concatenation, copied frozen-backbone bypass branches, zero-initialized residual injection, and scalar control strengths closely follow established control-adapter principles. The two-stage inference procedure is explicitly inherited from LTX-2. The multimodal integration could still justify publication, but stronger controlled evidence is needed to establish its distinctive benefit.

Important reproduction and evaluation details are missing. The manuscript does not specify the training loss and modality weighting, task-sampling proportions, temporal alignment between differently sampled audio/video latents, or how prepended reference tokens are mapped into target-length residual hints. It also leaves evaluation-set provenance, identity/source separation from training, baseline configurations, and depth normalization unclear. These omissions affect both implementation and interpretation of the reported gains.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 1 improves Sync-C but has worse Sync-D than Hallo3 (10.506 versus 10.243), so synchronization superiority is mixed. Some visual improvements are small and lack uncertainty estimates; the human study provides no confidence intervals and leaves the number of unique evaluated examples unclear. Comparing generated speech with methods driven by ground-truth speech also changes the synchronization task, rather than simply giving baselines an unambiguous advantage. Claims of perfect synchronization and state-of-the-art pose adherence should therefore be narrowed.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: combining reference identity, voice timbre, and structural conditioning within joint audio-video generation. Extending controllability beyond video alone has clear relevance to personalized content creation.

The architecture is coherent and plausibly implementable: modality-specific branches inject zero-initialized residuals into a frozen LTX-2 backbone. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges ControlNet-style conditioning and the inherited LTX-2 refinement procedure.

Depth-control results are promising. Table 2 reports MAE ×100 of 4.52 versus VACE’s 5.35, alongside improved subject similarity and dynamic degree. Qualitative examples also illustrate useful identity and structural adherence.

Evaluation includes complementary evidence from automatic visual and synchronization metrics, a 20-participant user study, and supplementary speech-quality measurements. Table 1 shows competitive performance, including the highest reported Sync-C, and the user study favors MMControl.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. There is no quantitative comparison with the underlying LTX-2 model, a straightforward ControlNet-style adaptation on the same backbone, or ablations of the MMCU masks, branch design, and cross-modal attention omission. Consequently, improvements over different generation systems cannot establish what the proposed components contribute beyond the strong pretrained backbone. This is consequential under the default Algorithms/General assessment.

The novelty is primarily an integration of established mechanisms: latent concatenation and masks, copied trainable bypass blocks, zero-initialized residual injection, and scalar control strengths. Such integration could be valuable, but the paper provides little controlled evidence showing why this particular design is necessary or preferable. The inherited two-stage LTX-2 inference procedure does not independently strengthen the originality claim.

Evidence for the central acoustic-control and composability claims is limited. Table S2 reports only absolute results on 150 examples—SIM-o 0.2574, UTMOS 3.49, and weighted WER 7.96%—without an uncontrolled-backbone comparison, reference calibration, or competing voice-conditioned system. Figure 7 supplies one qualitative binary on/off example, rather than quantitative guidance sweeps or tests of interference between modalities. Simultaneous identity, timbre, and structural control is not quantitatively established, and pose adherence receives no quantitative evaluation.

The baseline comparisons involve materially different tasks and conditioning. Audio-driven methods reproduce supplied speech, whereas MMControl generates both modalities and can choose mutually compatible speech timing and motion. Ground-truth audio is therefore not simply an advantage that makes the synchronization comparison conservative. Differences in backbone capacity and text-conditioning support also complicate attribution of visual and semantic gains. A matched joint-generation baseline and a competitive cascaded speech-plus-video pipeline would substantially strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility and evaluation validity remain unclear. The manuscript does not specify the training loss and modality weighting, task-sampling proportions, temporal alignment and positional treatment of differently sized reference streams, or sufficient generation settings. Benchmark provenance and identity/source-disjoint train-test splits are unspecified; non-overlapping reference and target audio within a clip does not establish benchmark independence. Depth normalization and baseline configurations also need clarification.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 1 gives worse Sync-D than Hallo3 (10.506 versus 10.243), so broad synchronization-superiority claims need qualification. Freezing the backbone does not guarantee preservation of its behavior after residual injection. No uncertainty estimates accompany the quantitative results, and the user study leaves sample overlap, randomization, and blinding unclear. These issues matter particularly for small gains such as subject DINO similarity and for claims of precise, independent control.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: jointly controlling visual identity, voice timbre, and motion or structure while generating synchronized audio and video. Bringing these controls into one model has practical value beyond video-only conditioning.

The architecture is coherent: modality-specific branches inject zero-initialized residual hints into a frozen joint backbone, retaining its cross-modal attention. The paper clearly acknowledges its use of LTX-2 and its existing two-stage inference procedure.
Depth-control results are promising. Table 2 reports depth MAE of 4.52 versus VACE’s 5.35, alongside improved subject similarity and dynamic degree, although aesthetic quality is lower.

The evaluation includes complementary evidence. Table 1 reports the best Sync-C among evaluated methods, and the 20-participant study reports an overall preference score of 3.58 versus 3.22 for Hallo3. Appendix B also evaluates speaker similarity, speech quality, and transcription accuracy on 150 samples.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological advance is insufficiently isolated. Latent concatenation with masks, ControlNet-style bypass branches, and residual scaling are established ingredients. There is no quantitative comparison against an appropriately conditioned LTX-2 baseline or a simpler adapter trained on the same data, and no architectural ablations. Consequently, improvements cannot be attributed convincingly to MMCU or the dual-stream design rather than the stronger backbone.

Evidence for the central composability and independent-control claims is limited. Training describes three conditioning tasks separately, but evaluation does not systematically test simultaneous identity, timbre, and structural control. Pose control is only qualitative. Figure 7 tests binary branch activation in one example; it does not establish continuous fidelity–creativity trade-offs or quantify cross-modal interference. Moreover, a single visual scale jointly affects identity and structure, rather than independently adjusting each visual condition as the abstract suggests.

Appendix B provides useful audio measurements but no comparison with the same model without audio conditioning, a matched alternative, or reference-audio quality. Thus, SIM-o of 0.2574 and UTMOS of 3.49 do not establish the effectiveness of timbre control. The speaker metric is also described as cosine distance while higher values are treated as better, leaving its definition ambiguous.

Baseline comparisons are informative but do not substantiate broad state-of-the-art claims. Audio-driven methods receive fixed ground-truth speech, whereas MMControl generates both modalities; this changes the synchronization problem, not merely its difficulty. Table 1 also shows worse Sync-D than Hallo3 (10.506 versus 10.243). A matched joint-generation baseline and a competitive cascaded system would better establish the benefit of the proposed approach.

Reproducibility and evaluation reliability remain concerns. The manuscript does not specify the training loss and modality weighting, temporal/positional alignment of reference and generated tokens, training resolution and duration, or sufficiently detailed inference settings. Test-set provenance and separation from training identities/videos are unspecified. Reported improvements lack uncertainty estimates, and the human-study description leaves the number of distinct evaluated clips and assignment/randomization procedure unclear.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: jointly controlling visual identity, voice timbre, and depth or pose while generating synchronized audio and video. Integrating these capabilities into one model has practical value beyond improving individual benchmark scores.

The architecture is coherent: modality-specific control branches inject zero-initialized residual hints into a frozen joint diffusion backbone, preserving its existing cross-modal interactions. The manuscript clearly credits LTX-2 for the backbone and progressive inference procedure.

The structural-control results are encouraging. MMControl improves depth MAE over VACE from 5.35 to 4.52 and pose MAE from 3.29 to 3.07. Appendix Table S5 also reports substantial improvements over the relevant concurrent AVControl framework.

The appendix provides meaningful supporting evidence rather than only qualitative examples. Table S3 tests masks, initialization, branch separation, and additional cross-attention; removing projector weight inheritance substantially degrades structural accuracy. The human study favors MMControl, and the audio evaluation includes speaker similarity, naturalness, and transcription accuracy.
weaknesses: The central claim of composable multimodal control is only partially tested. The reported training tasks and evaluations mainly cover image-plus-audio, image-plus-depth, and image-plus-pose separately. There is no clear quantitative evaluation of simultaneous image, reference-voice, and structural conditioning, or of independently selected visual and acoustic identities. These experiments are particularly important for establishing that the unified model supports the claimed combinations rather than several separate conditioning modes.

The evidence does not establish strong independence of the guidance controls. In Table S4, changing visual guidance from 1.0 to either 0.5 or 1.3 reduces speaker similarity from 0.22 to 0.16 despite fixed acoustic guidance. Increasing acoustic guidance to 1.3 also reduces speaker similarity to 0.14. This supports adjustable conditioning but qualifies the stronger claims of decoupled control and predictable adherence. A joint sweep measuring identity, timbre, structural fidelity, and synchronization would clarify the trade-offs.

Evaluation provenance and uncertainty are insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not explain the test-set sources or separation from training by source video and identity; non-overlapping reference and target audio segments alone do not establish held-out evaluation. The pose benchmark size, depth normalization, and pose-MAE computation are also unclear. Confidence intervals are absent, making small improvements such as pose MAE 3.29 to 3.07 difficult to assess. The human-study description leaves the number of unique evaluated clips ambiguous.

The comparisons only partly isolate the method's contribution. Most main-table baselines perform audio-driven animation or video-only control using different backbones and inputs. Their results demonstrate useful output quality but cannot establish that gains arise from MMCU rather than the strong LTX-2 prior. The AVControl comparison helps, but its training and inference configuration is unspecified. Audio scores in Table S2 lack a baseline or real-audio reference, while the no-audio-branch comparison in Table S3 provides only partial calibration. The synchronization superiority claim also needs qualification because Hallo3 obtains better Sync-D.

Reproducibility and methodological differentiation need more detail. The training loss, relative audio/video loss weights, task sampling, temporal alignment of unequal audio/video latent sequences, output resolution and duration, and reference-audio length are not adequately documented. Trainable parameter counts and inference costs are missing despite efficiency claims. Since the main mechanisms closely resemble established bypass conditioning, masked reference concatenation, and residual scaling, a sharper explanation of the technical advance over these ingredients and AVControl is needed. Overall, the promising results make this a close decision, but the central compositional-control claims remain insufficiently validated.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: jointly generating video and speech while controlling visual identity, voice timbre, and scene structure. Integrating these controls into a single pretrained audio-video model has practical value.

The architecture is coherent: modality-specific branches, pretrained initialization, and zero-initialized residual projections provide a plausible way to add conditioning while preserving the frozen backbone. The manuscript clearly acknowledges that its two-stage inference procedure comes from LTX-2.

Structural-control results are promising. MMControl improves depth MAE over VACE from 5.35 to 4.52 and pose MAE from 3.29 to 3.07. Appendix D also includes a relevant comparison with concurrent AVControl, reporting substantially lower structural errors.

The supplementary evaluation adds meaningful evidence beyond visual examples. Table S3 tests masks, projector initialization, branch removal, and cross-modal attention; the results support several design choices. The human study favors MMControl, and the audio evaluation measures speaker similarity, naturalness, and intelligibility.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological advance is limited and insufficiently isolated. MMCU primarily concatenates reference/control latents and masks; the bypass branches closely follow established ControlNet-style initialization and residual injection; guidance scaling multiplies residual features by scalar weights. Extending these mechanisms to joint audio-video generation is useful, but the paper needs stronger evidence of what this particular integration contributes beyond LTX-2 and standard adapters. The AVControl comparison helps, but does not establish this under matched training and computational budgets.

The evidence does not adequately establish independent, composable control, a central claim. Training describes three paired conditioning tasks, while quantitative results largely evaluate these separately. There is no clear quantitative test jointly combining reference identity, reference timbre, and depth or pose, or recombining identities and voices from different sources. Moreover, Table S4 shows that changing visual guidance from 1.0 to either 0.5 or 1.3 reduces speaker similarity from 0.22 to 0.16; increasing acoustic guidance to 1.3 reduces it to 0.14. These results demonstrate adjustable conditioning but do not establish reliable independence or progressively stronger timbre adherence.

Comparisons do not sufficiently separate backbone capability from the proposed control mechanism. Table 1 compares a 19B joint generator against audio-driven animation systems performing a different task with supplied speech. The distinction is disclosed, but generating its own speech can also change the synchronization problem, so ground-truth audio is not simply an advantage for the baselines. A matched LTX-2 conditioning baseline and a competitive voice-generation-plus-animation pipeline would provide much stronger evidence. Table S2 reports only MMControl's absolute audio scores, leaving the significance of its timbre-control performance unclear.

Benchmark construction and statistical reliability are underspecified. The manuscript does not clearly identify test-data provenance, subject/speaker separation from training, the main pose evaluation sample count, or selection procedures for the supplementary subsets. Non-overlapping reference and target segments address within-example leakage but do not establish train/test independence. No uncertainty estimates are given, including for small differences such as pose MAE 3.07 versus 3.29. The human study reports 20 participants rating five instances per method, but leaves the number of unique instances, assignment, blinding, and uncertainty unclear.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the training loss and relative audio/video weighting, training and output resolutions and durations, task sampling proportions, and the temporal/positional alignment of reference-prefixed control tokens with backbone tokens. Depth normalization and the definition of pose MAE are also insufficiently specified. Reporting 12 hours on four H200 GPUs is helpful, but without trainable parameter counts, inference cost, or matched comparisons, it does not substantiate the efficiency claims.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 1 favors MMControl on Sync-C but favors Hallo3 on Sync-D, so claims of superior synchronization require qualification. The experiments primarily concern speaking characters and do not establish broad multimodal generalization. Overall, the promising structural results and component ablations support feasibility, but important gaps remain in validating the submission's main claims of independent control and improved joint generation.

strengths: The paper addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: jointly controlling visual identity, voice timbre, and spatial structure during synchronized audio-video generation. Bringing these capabilities into one framework has practical significance beyond improving individual benchmark scores.

The architecture is coherent and clearly motivated. Modality-specific bypass branches, masked reference conditioning, and zero-initialized residual projections provide a plausible way to add control while retaining a frozen joint generative backbone.

Structural-control results are promising. MMControl improves depth MAE over VACE from 5.35 to 4.52 and pose MAE from 3.29 to 3.07. The additional AVControl comparison in Table S5 strengthens the evidence by including a closely related joint audio-video control framework.

The supplementary component ablations provide useful support for the design: removing projector initialization substantially degrades structural adherence, and removing the audio bypass reduces speaker similarity. The human study also favors MMControl, with an overall score of 3.58 versus 3.22 for the strongest baseline.
weaknesses: The central voice-timbre contribution lacks a convincing comparative evaluation. Table S2 reports only MMControl's speaker similarity, naturalness, and WER, without an unconditioned LTX-2 reference or a competitive voice-conditioned synthesis pipeline. Table S3 establishes that the audio branch helps, but does not establish competitive timbre fidelity. Quantitative evidence for simultaneously combining voice reference, visual identity, and structural control is also limited.

The claim of independent modality control is stronger than the evidence supports. In Table S4, changing visual guidance from 1.0 to either 0.5 or 1.3 reduces speaker similarity from 0.22 to 0.16. Increasing acoustic guidance to 1.3 also reduces speaker similarity to 0.14. These results demonstrate sensitivity and cross-modal interaction, rather than reliable independent adjustment of reference adherence.

The main comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the proposed method from the pretrained backbone. Table 1 compares joint synthesis against methods driven by ground-truth audio, with different architectures and generation tasks. This comparison is informative but cannot attribute synchronization gains specifically to MMControl. A matched LTX-2 control-adapter baseline would better establish the benefit over standard conditioning mechanisms.

Reproducibility and evaluation details are incomplete. The manuscript does not specify the training loss and modality weighting, training resolution and duration, or sufficiently explain alignment between reference-prefixed control tokens and backbone tokens. Test-set provenance, speaker/identity separation from training, pose-error computation, and depth normalization are also unclear. Non-overlapping reference and target audio segments do not establish train-test independence.

Several improvements need more cautious interpretation. Table 1 improves Sync-C but not Sync-D relative to Hallo3, and the pose-MAE improvement over VACE is modest without uncertainty estimates. The small human study lacks confidence intervals and clear reporting of unique evaluated samples. Algorithmic novelty is principally an adaptation of established bypass conditioning and residual scaling to joint generation; stronger controlled evidence is therefore important. Overall, the promising integration falls slightly short of acceptance because its central acoustic and compositional claims remain insufficiently validated.
